title: Sabzi polo
subtitle: Persian herb rice for Nowruz
excerpt: Sabzi polo is a fragrant Persian rice made with a generous abundance of fresh herbs. Parsley, coriander, dill, and fenugreek leaves are folded through rice at every layer, giving it a brilliant green flecked interior and an extraordinary herby scent. It is the centrepiece of the Persian New Year table.
sourceNotes: A central dish of Nowruz (Persian New Year, around the spring equinox). Traditionally served with herb-stuffed fish (mahi) or simply with yoghurt and pickles. The herbs symbolise new growth and spring.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made and served fresh. The tahdig will soften in the fridge.

content.text: The herb quantity in sabzi polo looks almost absurd at first. You are using 200 g of fresh herbs for four people, and the pile looks enormous. Once the herbs go into the steam with the rice they collapse entirely and the finished dish is warmly herbal rather than raw or bitter.

What makes this rice special is the tahdig: the crisp, golden crust that forms on the base of the pot. Inverting the pot onto a plate reveals a dome of green rice with a golden crown, which is the moment sabzi polo becomes worth all the effort.

Fenugreek leaves (methi) are an essential element, not optional. Without them the dish lacks its characteristic slightly bitter edge. Dried fenugreek leaves work if fresh are not available; use 2 tablespoons of dried.

items.prepNote: dried; or 30 g fresh fenugreek leaves
mixed with 2 spoonfuls of rice to form the tahdig base

content.text: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Drain the soaked rice and add to the water. Boil for 6 minutes until two-thirds cooked: no longer chalky but still firm in the centre. Drain well in a colander and rinse with cold water. Mix in the chopped herbs and dried fenugreek while the rice is still warm. Toss gently to combine.

Melt the butter in a heavy-based pot over medium heat. Mix the yoghurt with 2 large spoonfuls of the herb-rice mixture and press this into the base of the pot in an even layer. This is the tahdig, which will form the crisp base crust.

Mound the remaining herb-rice over the tahdig layer, building it into a loose pyramid shape. Drizzle the saffron water over the top if using. Wrap the pot lid in a clean tea towel and cover tightly. Cook over a medium heat for 5 minutes until you hear a light sizzle, then reduce to the lowest possible heat and cook for 40 minutes. To unmould, set the pot base briefly in cold water for 30 seconds, then invert onto a large plate.

rows.cause: Heat too high for the steaming stage
rows.fix: After the initial 5 minutes, reduce to the absolute minimum. Use a heat diffuser if available.
The herbs should stay bright green with gentle steaming; if they are turning dark, the heat is too high.

rows.cause: Parboiled too long or too much water left on the rice
rows.fix: Drain very thoroughly after parboiling and rinse with cold water; excess moisture makes the finished rice dense.

content.text: Sabzi polo is traditionally served with herb-stuffed fish (mahi), which is also a Nowruz staple. Plain roasted chicken or lamb chops are simpler alternatives. For a dried herb version in winter, use a combination of dried dill, dried parsley, and dried coriander; the flavour is less vivid but still good.
Sabzi polo should be made and served fresh on the day. The parboiled and herb-mixed rice can be prepared a few hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature; finish in the pot close to serving.

Sabzi polo mahi is one of the most important dishes of Nowruz, the Persian New Year. The green herbs stand for rebirth and spring. It is made in Iranian households across Iran and throughout the diaspora around the world, and is one of the dishes that most strongly marks Persian cultural identity in the kitchen.
